sources.title: Herbert Franke: The Chin dynasty, Cambridge History of China
sources.note: Publisher chapter summary directly indexed and read: Jurchen identity, 1115-1234, conquest of Liao, northern China, comparative government. Not claiming access to the full paywalled chapter.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of China: Jin Dynasty, 1115-1234
sources.note: Publisher original page and indexed full article read. Opening: Aguda1115, move to Beijing1153, Kaifeng1214, Caizhou and Mongol-Song defeat1234. sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: A Diplomatic Mission to the Jin
sources.note: Direct indexed catalogue, 1982.1.1, attributed Yang Bangji, ca. late1150s, ink/color on silk. 1127 conquest and possible Song envoy subject; identification explicitly uncertain. Tribute quantities not adopted.

sources.title: Tao Jing-shen: The Influence of Jurchen Rule on Chinese Political Institutions
sources.note: Publisher original abstract, Journal of Asian Studies. Successor role of Jin to Northern Song and transfer of institutions to later conquest dynasties; public summary stays within abstract.

sources.title: Xin Wen: The Road to Literary Culture, Revisiting the Jurchen Language Examination System
sources.note: T’oung Pao101(2015),130-167. Direct repository fetch failed; indexed original PDF p142 reproduced with site:scholar.harvard.edu "Jurchen" "Baozhou". Read1164translation project,1169-70LouYue school sign,1173first exams and minimum500characters. p149 indexed original verified expansion. Scholarly article copy indexed elsewhere helped navigation but original query supports public passages.

sources.title: University of Michigan Museum of Art: Tiger-shaped pillow
sources.note: Direct catalogue1993/1.103, Jin1115-1234, stoneware/slip, Henan/Shanxi kilns; curator explains hard neck rests could protect elaborate coiffures. Avoid claiming all users or all pillows had one purpose.

sources.title: Montreal Museum of Fine Arts: Cizhou Pillow
sources.note: Direct catalogue, Jin, octagonal pillow with bird on bamboo, white slip/transparent glaze/iron-black paint and Zhang family base stamp. Transliteration label used only as craft attribution, no reconstructed Chinese mark.

sources.title: Pengliang Lu: Cruel Elegance in an Eight-Hundred-Year-Old Chinese Brocade
sources.note: Direct curator essay23December2015; object1989.282, twelfth-thirteenth century; green silk, gilded parchment strips, swan/falcon motif and historical noblemen spring-hunt robes. Public prose restricts custom to elite men.

sources.title: National Office for Philosophy and Social Sciences: Jin artifacts and literary research
sources.note: Direct Chinese project report, numbered conclusion1. Dong Ming tomb, Houma, brick stage and five actor figures; Houma ErshuiM4 ink inscriptions with three surviving zhugongdiao song fragments. Speculative author/family relationship not used.

sources.title: History of Jin: Biography of Liu Wansu, chapter131
sources.note: Primary dynastic history written after Jin fall, preserved in Chinese Text Project transcription. Direct403; indexed Chinese original and English translation read under 劉完素: multiple medical books and 好用涼劑. Legendary revelation by intoxication not adopted; treatment theory is historical, no efficacy or present advice.

sources.title: Miyazawa Tomoyuki: The Monetary System During the First Half of the Jin Dynasty
sources.note: Kyoto University original indexed English abstract,2020, Toyoshi kenkyu79(2),205-235, DOI10.14989/285263. Early system before1190s, Northern Song coins inherited, uneven cash holdings, jiaochao interpreted as deposit/remittance drafts rather than ordinary paper money. Direct page no extracted text; full abstract indexed.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art: Wind and Snow in the Fir Pines
sources.note: Direct collectionF1961.34a-c. LiShan, late12thcentury; Artist Inscription4 exact平陽李山製, translated Made by Li Shan of Pingyang. Distinguish artist signature from later labels, Qing imperial poem and subsequent colophons.

sources.title: Jinping Wang: In the Wake of the Mongols, Harvard-Yenching Institute
sources.note: Direct author monograph description2018:1211-1234conquest, stone inscriptions documenting adaptation in Shanxi and roles of priests, monks and women. Population-loss estimate not reproduced as settled census.
